question: Let S and T be Hermitian matrices on one finite system and X a Hermitian matrix on a second system. Prove that H=S tensor X+T tensor I is Hermitian without assuming that S and T commute. Give a counterexample showing that the same conclusion can fail if X is not Hermitian.
reference_answer: The adjoint of a tensor product is the tensor product of the adjoints: entrywise, conjugating S(j,i)X(v,u) gives S(i,j)X(u,v) under Hermiticity of both factors. Hence (S tensor X) dagger=S tensor X. Similarly T tensor I is Hermitian because I dagger=I. Adjoint is additive, so H dagger=H. No product S T occurs anywhere in this argument, so S and T need not commute. The premise on X matters: take the first system one-dimensional with S=[1], T=[0], and X=[[0,1],[0,0]]. Then H=X, whereas X dagger=[[0,0],[1,0]] is different. This is an operator-algebra closure result, not a claim that implementing the factors or reading out a simulated evolution is free.

Explicitly do not assume S and T commute
Valid non-Hermitian counterexample when X premise removed

All declared products have compatible dimensions

question: A finite row stencil is a list of offset/coefficient pairs. Its matrix entry at row i and column j is the sum of coefficients of every pair with i+offset=j; no modular wrapping is used. Prove that merging repeated offsets by summing their coefficients leaves every matrix entry unchanged. Use the pairs (1,2),(1,-2),(-1,3) to show why list width and the number of nonzero matrix entries need not agree.
reference_answer: Fix i,j. Every pair contributes its coefficient if its offset equals j-i and contributes zero otherwise. Group the finite sum by equal offsets; associativity and commutativity of scalar addition preserve the sum. Replacing each group by a single pair whose coefficient is that group sum therefore gives exactly the same entry for this arbitrary i,j, hence the same matrix. In the example the offset1 coefficient is2-2=0, while the offset-1 coefficient is3. Thus the entry at j=i+1 vanishes and the entry at j=i-1 equals3 if that column lies in the finite grid. The original list has three pairs, its merged list can have two pairs including a zero, and it has at most one nonzero matrix entry in a row; at a left boundary even that entry may disappear because j=i-1 is outside the grid. An access permutation or sparse-oracle cost cannot be inferred solely from the unmerged list length. This proof uses the stated additive matrix semantics, not a claim that arbitrary loaders with collided labels are automatically reversible.

Distinguish list count, actual support and boundary truncation without claiming free access
